questions.q: According to this lesson, where should you look first when checking on a production Airflow deployment?
options: The Airflow installation's server hardware logs
A third-party monitoring dashboard unrelated to Airflow
The Grid view — a run-by-run, task-by-task colored status history
The DAG's raw Python source file
questions.explain: The Grid view gives an at-a-glance run history across tasks and runs, making it the first place to check task health.

questions.q: In the Grid view, what does a single red cell in an otherwise all-green row most likely indicate, compared to a row that fails every third run?
options: Both situations mean exactly the same thing
The DAG has been deleted
The entire Airflow installation has crashed
An isolated failure, as opposed to a recurring pattern that likely needs deeper investigation
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes an isolated failure (one red cell) from a pattern (a row trending red), which determines whether you fix one task or investigate something upstream.

questions.q: What does clicking into a task instance's Logs tab actually show you?
options: The real, timestamped text output from that specific run, including any exception traceback
A list of every other DAG in the deployment
A generic summary with no actual output
Only the DAG's schedule interval
questions.explain: The Logs tab shows real output produced during that exact run — not a summary — including a full traceback if the task raised an exception.

questions.q: According to this lesson, which direction should you read a task's log when hunting for a failure?
options: Always from the very first line only
From the bottom up first, since the most recent lines usually show the actual failure
Alphabetically by line content
Logs should never be read; only the color of the Grid cell matters
questions.explain: Reading from the bottom up first surfaces the actual failure (exception or non-zero exit) faster than wading through earlier setup noise.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is monitoring, fundamentally?
options: Something that only matters during initial DAG development, not after deployment
A habit built entirely on the existing Airflow UI, not a separate tool bolted on
A one-time setup step with no ongoing practice involved
A completely separate paid product unrelated to the Airflow UI
questions.explain: The lesson frames monitoring as an ongoing habit of checking the Grid and reading logs — using the same UI already covered, not a separate system.
